scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The pas de deux emerged in the mid-18th century within the 'ballet d'action' and reached its formal peak during the 19th-century Romantic era.
Marius Petipa is credited with codifying the five-part structure that remains the standard for the grand pas de deux.
While early versions focused on synchronized steps, the form evolved to emphasize the romantic partnership and the distinct technical capabilities of the ballerina and the danseur.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The pas de deux is often the pièce de résistance of a ballet, frequently symbolizing a love story or the emotional connection between two characters.
It is used to illustrate the most poetic moments of a narrative.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed by a pair, typically a male and female.
The ballerina often dances on pointe, requiring advanced strength.
The danseur provides support, acting as a 'third leg' to balance, lift, and turn the ballerina.
Watch for Promenade, Pirouettes, Portée.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Marius Petipa is the primary figure in the codification of the form.
Contemporary choreographers like Maurice Béjart, George Balanchine, Akram Khan, and Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui have adapted the form for modern contexts.

While the grand pas de deux is a global standard in classical ballet, contemporary choreographers often refer to their works as 'duos' rather than 'pas de deux' to reflect a shift away from traditional structures.
The form is a direct descendant of the 18th-century 'entrée de ballet' and evolved through the Romantic ballet period into the 19th-century classical standard.
